title: Inquest into man's 2018 death in Meadow Lake RCMP detention cell begins
subtitle: An inquest into the April 2018 death of 25-year-old Trevor McCallum began in Saskatoon on Monday.
article: A 25-year-old man whose death is the subject of a coroners inquest had removed his clothes and was pacing in his cell hours before he was found unresponsive in the Meadow Lake RCMP detention area, the jury heard Monday.

Trevor McCallum, a father of two, was found unresponsive shortly before 6 a.m. on April 10, 2018 and was pronounced dead by paramedics at the scene, according to RCMP in a news release issued two days later. Police did not identify McCallum in the release.
McCallum's death was later found to be the result of an overdose, coroner's counsel Robin Ritter told the inquest. A forensic pathologist is expected to testify this week.
Testimony began Monday after the six-person jury was selected from two jury pools - one comprised of prospective Indigenous jurors and the other comprised of non-Indigenous candidates.

Under provincial legislation , if the chief coroner believes the circumstances of a death require the jury to be composed "wholly or in part, of persons from a specific racial or cultural group," prospective jurors can be summoned accordingly. A similar process was used for the 2018 inquest into Jordan Lafond's death following a fatal police pursuit in Saskatoon.

Const. Jared Rau, the first witness to testify, recalled looking at video surveillance from McCallum's cell during his 5 p.m. to 3 a.m. shift on April 9. McCallum, who had been brought in earlier that day, was pacing in the cell and there were torn pieces of paper on the ground, Rau said.
"For Trevor, I would say that's normal behaviour," Rau told the inquest.

Rau said when he went to the cellblock and looked into McCallum's cell, he saw the papers were pages from a book. He could not recall the time, but testified to being told by a guard that McCallum had a cellmate who had been moved.

Const. Kenneth Wilkins, also working the overnight shift, testified to moving McCallum's cellmate to another cell at the man's request. He testified to seeing McCallum sitting shirtless in his cell at about 7 p.m., and described McCallum as being somewhere between "belligerent and rude."
Rau said members now have to check people in the detention cells at the end of their shifts.
A third officer who testified, Const. Jonathan Griffioen, told the inquest that if 24-hour policing were in place at the detachment at the time, the outcome may have been different.

Griffioen was the first RCMP member who entered McCallum's cell the morning of April 10. He had been dispatched just before 6 a.m. when McCallum was reported unresponsive. Paramedics were already at the scene.
He described finding McCallum laying on his back and said he was cool to the touch, unresponsive and stiff. He didn't believe McCallum was still alive, Griffioen testified.

Griffioen said a guard on duty told him he tried to splash McCallum with water through an opening in the cell door when the guard found him unresponsive. He said the guard said he poked McCallum with a broom.
Griffioen and Rau testified to knowing McCallum was a user of cocaine, possibly crystal meth, and that each had taken McCallum to a hospital in the past on more than one occasion.
Present in the gallery were members of McCallum's family, including his mother who has standing to question witnesses.
Roseanne McCallum described her son in a previous interview as a very good person who kept his word .

The inquest is scheduled to continue Tuesday. An inquest is a fact-finding, not fault-finding, process that establishes when and how someone died. It may also highlight dangerous conditions or practices, and the jury can make non-binding recommendations to prevent future deaths.
